query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A moderate post-deposition vacuum heat treatment at around 500 °C promotes the formation of a continuous, protective composite oxide layer (rich in Cr2O3 and Cu-oxide phases) on FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings, which increases hardness and reduces abrasive and adhesive wear at high temperatures. In contrast, treatments at higher temperatures lead to full recrystallization and grain coarsening, reducing hardness and wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu thin protective coating (single-phase high-entropy alloy microstructure without significant oxide surface layers).
generation.intervention: Apply a vacuum heat treatment at ~500 °C to the as-sprayed coating.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear environment (around 500–700 °C) under conditions simulating service loads (e.g., sliding wear or impact conditions typical of high-temperature protective applications).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a heterogeneous, adherent oxide layer (primarily Cr2O3 combined with Cu-oxide spinels) that reinforces surface hardness.
generation.mechanism: At moderate temperatures (≈500 °C), limited thermal energy promotes diffusion-driven surface oxidation and nanotwin/dislocation formation without complete recrystallization. This leads to a tough, composite oxide layer that acts as a solid lubricant barrier reducing metal-to-metal contact and wear. In contrast, higher temperature treatments can lead to full recrystallization, grain coarsening, and decreased microhardness, which diminish wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The 500 °C heat-treated coatings will exhibit higher microhardness and lower specific wear rates under high-temperature wear tests compared to as-sprayed (room temperature baseline) coatings, while those treated at higher temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C) will show degraded wear resistance.
generation.baseline: The as-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating without any heat treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in high-temperature wear environments up to around 700 °C; beyond this boundary, complete recrystallization and grain coarsening likely negate the benefits of the protective oxide formation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and protective efficiency of the oxide layer in FeNiCrCoCu specifically is not fully established, and variations in deposition method or environmental oxygen availability may influence the oxide phase formation and the subsequent wear behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin protective coatings: one set as-sprayed (baseline) and one set subjected to a 500 °C vacuum heat treatment. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature wear tests (e.g., sliding wear test at 600 °C under standardized normal loads). Characterize the surface morphology and composition (focusing on oxide layer formation) using SEM and XPS, and measure microhardness and specific wear rates.
measurements: Volume wear rate (mm^3·N^−1·m^−1) during high-temperature wear tests
Surface oxide layer composition and continuity (SEM/XPS analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 500 °C heat-treated coatings do not show a statistically significant increase in microhardness and a reduction in wear rate relative to the as-sprayed coatings—or if no distinct protective oxide layer forms—the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Phase Structure and Morphology of CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy Coating
cited_evidence.text: Figure 7 shows the microhardness distribution curves of CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings prepared by CS and HVOF, and the coatings heat-treated at different temperatures. Both coatings reach the highest hardness at 500 °C, 487.6 HV0.1 for CS coating and 352.4 HV0.1 for HVOF coating. At 700 °C and 900 °C, the hardness of both coatings is lower than that at room temperature. This is because the heat treatment at 500 °C makes the coating form a heterogeneous structure composed of nanotwins in the recrystallized grains, and high-density dislocations appear in the deformation region. When the annealing temperature exceeds 500 °C, the coating exhibits a completely recrystallized structure, the yield stress decreases and the hardness decreases.

The wear rates of the two coatings at room temperature are very close. The wear rate for the CS and HVOF coatings reaches its the lowest point after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C. The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm3 m−1 N−1, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm3 m−1 N−1) of that of the HVOF-500 °C coating. The CS coating with 500 °C vacuum heat treatment has the best wear resistance due to having the highest microhardness. The wear rates and wear amounts of the two coatings heat-treated at 700 °C and 900 °C decreases due to the decrease in microhardness. The wear mechanisms of the CS and HVOF coatings before and after vacuum heat treatment are adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear and oxidation wear.
